title: Neural Sources and Underlying Mechanisms of Neural Responses to Heartbeats, and their Role in Bodily Self-consciousness: An Intracranial EEG Study
post: Aim: Whether heartbeat-evoked potentials arise from neural sources and mechanisms that can be localised, and whether they relate to bodily self-consciousness. Methods: Two intracranial EEG experiments in patients, examining heartbeat-locked phase distributions and spectral power across recording sites, and HEP modulation during an experimentally induced altered sense of self-identification. Results: Shortly after heartbeat onset, phases were significantly concentrated in about 10% of sites, mainly insula and operculum, without increased spectral power, suggesting phase resetting. Insula HEP modulations reflected altered self-identification. Conclusion: The authors conclude that HEPs arise largely through phase resetting and that their insular modulation supports a functional role in self-consciousness.
why_you: Directly relevant to your interest in heart-brain coupling and interoception, offering intracranial evidence on where cardiac-evoked responses originate.

title: Increased signal diversity/complexity of spontaneous EEG, but not evoked EEG responses, in ketamine-induced psychedelic state in humans
post: Aim: Whether EEG signal diversity, measured spontaneously and evoked by TMS, changes under sub-anaesthetic ketamine and relates to subjective experience. Methods: Open-label within-subject study in 10 healthy volunteers with 62-channel EEG, recording TMS-evoked responses (PCI) and spontaneous EEG (Lempel-Ziv complexity, amplitude and synchrony coalition entropy) before and during sub-anaesthetic ketamine. Results: No significant change in evoked complexity (PCI). All spontaneous signal diversity measures increased under ketamine, correlating with subjective altered states, and were higher with eyes open than closed. Conclusion: Spontaneous and evoked complexity may reflect complementary aspects; ketamine may raise conscious-content complexity while leaving overall capacity for consciousness largely unchanged.
why_you: Directly matches your work on ketamine, EEG complexity and TMS-EEG perturbation measures.

title: Genome writing reveals SVA retrotransposon consequences in X-linked dystonia-parkinsonism.
post: Aim: How an intronic SVA retrotransposon in TAF1 contributes to X-linked dystonia-parkinsonism (XDP). Methods: Genomic rewriting of a portion of the mouse Taf1 allele with the 78-kb XDP patient-derived allele in mouse embryonic stem cells and mice, with chromatin and transcriptome profiling and CRISPRa activation. Results: The intronic SVA reduced hybrid TAF1 mRNA, downregulated TATA-box genes and triggered apoptosis. Intronic SVAs were actively transcribed and impeded elongation. Neuronal humanisation caused male lethality and striatal atrophy, and CRISPRa activation restored viability. Conclusion: Boosting TAF1 transcription may be a therapeutic approach for XDP, which is associated with striatal degeneration.

title: A thalamo-amygdalar circuit drives female vulnerability to chronic pain after early-life stress.
post: Aim: Whether early-life stress and nerve injury interact to produce female-specific circuit sensitisation driving chronic pain vulnerability. Methods: Mouse study of social isolation and nerve injury, measuring synaptic gain and activity in the paraventricular thalamus to central amygdala pathway, with chemogenetic inhibition and activation. Results: Social isolation plus nerve injury amplified synaptic gain and anticipatory recruitment of the pathway in female but not male mice. Pathway inhibition rescued behaviour, while sustained or phasic activation induced hypersensitivity or avoidance. Conclusion: A latent thalamo-amygdalar synaptic gain state, unmasked by injury, may transform early-life stress into female-specific vulnerability to chronic pain and anxiety-like avoidance.

title: A shared interbacterial membrane underlies mycobacterial cording.
post: Aim: How individual mycobacterial cells coordinate growth, division and adhesion to form serpentine cords. Methods: Live-cell fluorescence microscopy combined with cryo-electron tomography of virulent mycobacteria. Lipid composition and an interleaflet density associated with virulence-factor secretion were observed in M. tuberculosis. Conclusion: A multi-bacterial membrane architecture provides the structural basis for cording and collective behaviours such as mechanical stability and phage resistance.

title: Rhodopsin 7 is an ancestral non-canonical photoreceptor that shapes light-responsive behavior.
post: Aim: Whether Rhodopsin 7, a widely expressed non-canonical photoreceptor, shapes light-responsive behaviour in Drosophila. Methods: Expression mapping, behavioural assays of activity under light and dark, constitutively active RH7 strains, and phylogenetic comparisons across arthropods. Results: RH7 detects temporal luminance changes and guides rapid responses. Flies lacking RH7 were less active in the dark phase, while constitutively active RH7 increased activity. RH7 appears ancient across panarthropods. Conclusion: RH7 acts as a melanopsin-like sensor shaping behaviour and represents an evolutionary intermediate in non-visual light perception.

title: Nitric oxide feedback to ciliary photoreceptor cells gates a UV avoidance circuit.

title: Morally motivated crimes are less sensitive to punishment.
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
venue_clean: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
post: Aim: Whether morally motivated crimes are less sensitive to punishment than materially motivated ones. Methods: Ten studies combining federal offender data (over 30,000 offenders), judgment experiments and economic games with general-population and offender participants. Results: Moral motives predicted higher recidivism while material motives predicted lower recidivism. Morally motivated crimes were less sensitive to punishment across crime types and consequence manipulations, and players taking money for moral reasons were less deterred by fines. Conclusion: Punishment may deter morally motivated offending less effectively, with implications for sentencing and restorative justice approaches.

Methods: Single-neuron recordings from ACC (area 24) in freely moving marmosets engaged in spontaneous vocal exchanges within a colony setting. Results: ACC neurons selectively encoded calls from a social partner versus other callers, preserved during temporal overlap. Population activity also represented vocal production, call type and turn-taking context. Conclusion: ACC neurons appear to parse conspecific speakers during natural communication, linking auditory scene analysis with social monitoring.

title: Linguistic contextualization in the human hippocampus.
post: Aim: Whether hippocampal neurons encode word position and context in a way resembling transformer self-attention, in natural speech. Methods: Single-unit recordings from the human hippocampus in n = 10 participants listening to podcasts; analysis of positional encoding and weighted sums of preceding word embeddings, compared with LLM self-attention weights. Results: Hippocampal neurons encoded word position within a clause using ordinal and frequency-domain positional encoding. Neural responses reflected both a word's lexical semantics and a weighted sum of preceding word embeddings, with weights correlating with LLM self-attention. Conclusion: Contextualisation in the brain may use vectorial shifts resembling attentional reweighting in LLMs, highlighting the mesial temporal lobe in the language network.

title: Generational gains in cognitive capacity and dementia incidence rates in Western countries.
post: Aim: To test whether later-born generations enter old age with better memory and decline more slowly, and whether this explains falling dementia incidence. Methods: Analysis of about 783,000 episodic-memory assessments from about 219,000 individuals in five longitudinal studies followed up to 30 years, including hippocampal volumes. Results: Later-born generations showed higher memory levels in old age and slower subsequent decline, a double advantage large enough to plausibly account for the reported 13% per-decade fall in dementia incidence. Slower decline was mirrored by lower clinical impairment and slower hippocampal atrophy. Conclusion: Sustaining the dementia decline requires prevention that protects brain health across the lifespan, starting in childhood.

title: A shared meaning component across languages in the human brain.
post: Background: Human languages differ profoundly in their sounds, words and grammatical systems, yet all support the communication of complex meanings. Methods: Leveraging these advances, we evaluated the similarity of linguistic representations in speakers of 21 languages. Results: Model representations predicted brain responses reliably within each language. Critically, encoding models trained on one set of languages generalized zero-shot to previously unseen languages, accurately predicting neural responses without exposure to the target language. Conclusion: These findings point to a shared cross-lingual component for meaning across human languages.

title: Rainforest adaptation in late Homo erectus from southern China.
post: Background: Homo erectus represents one of the longest-persisting hominin species, with a geographic range from Africa to eastern Eurasia from approximately 1.9 million years ago1 to 108 thousand years ago (ka)2. Methods: Here we present a rich temporal and environmental context for nine hominin teeth, eight of which were morphologically and genetically identified as H. erectus5, found in two sister caves in Guangxi province, southern China. Results: We show that H. erectus was present in southern China between 324 and 184 ka, which is substantially more recent than previously established in this region for unequivocally H. erectus fossils at approximately 400 ka. Conclusion: The evidence suggests that they were persisting in closed rainforest ecosystems, thought to be the domain of only Homo sapiens, and were demonstrating long-term mobility and ecological flexibility.

title: Handling Incomplete Multimodal Data in ASD Diagnosis: A Masked Autoencoder Approach With Sex-Stratified Fusion.
post: Aim: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) diagnosis remains challenging due to heterogeneous phenotypic presentations and the inherent complexity of neurodevelopmental patterns. Methods: We propose a novel Missing-Modality-Robust Multimodal Fusion Framework (MMR-MF 3 ) that addresses these challenges through three key innovations. Results: Third, we implement sex-stratified classification heads that account for neurobiological sex differences, improving diagnostic accuracy across demographic groups. Finding: Our framework achieves state-of-the-art performance on Autism Brain Imaging Data Exchange (ABIDE) I and II datasets, with AUC of 0.89 for males and 0.86 for females. Conclusion: The proposed framework represents a significant advancement toward clinically deployable ASD diagnostic tools.

title: A Data-Driven Method to Map the Functional Organisation of Human Brain White Matter.
post: Background: Although diffusion MRI (dMRI) enables detailed mapping of these pathways through tractography, how WM pathways directly facilitate large-scale neural synchronisation remains poorly understood. Methods: We developed a data-driven framework that integrates dMRI and functional MRI (fMRI) to model the dynamic coupling supported by WM tracks. Results: Importantly, specific clusters encompassing pathways linking control, default mode, attention and visual systems significantly mediated the relationship between age and cognitive performance. Conclusion: Together, these findings depict the whole-brain track-level functional organisation of WM tracks and provide a powerful tool to study brain ageing and cognitive decline.

title: Dissociating Early Heartbeat-Evoked Afferent Gating From Late Associative Failure in Post-Anoxic Coma
post: Aim: Whether the heartbeat-evoked response can separate viable from non-viable cortical function in comatose patients after cardiac arrest. Results: Good outcome was linked to a preserved frontocentral deflection near 200 ms localised to the anterior cingulate and anterior insula, with high instantaneous energy and phase alignment. title: Meditation-induced coherence and perennial aging.
post: Aim: Examine how meditation alters scaling behaviour and complexity synchronisation between brain and heart dynamics, using a non-Markovian quantum-like framework. post: Aim: How the strength of interoceptive meaning in verbs shapes the spatiotemporal neural dynamics of conceptual processing. post: Aim: Systematically review randomised trials of yoga's physiological effects on sleep architecture and autonomic regulation, using objective endpoints. post: Aim: Whether the functional brain changes produced by eight weeks of taVNS in major depression map onto specific gene expression and neurotransmitter receptor patterns. title: Cross-cohort validation of EEG biomarkers using a pre-registered three-criterion framework: a demonstration in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
post: Aim: To develop and demonstrate a pre-registered three-criterion framework for identifying EEG features that show discrimination, reliability and cross-cohort consistency in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. title: Low-Threshold Intermittent Hypoxia Exacerbates LPS-Induced Depressive-Like Behaviors and Cognitive Deficits While Potentiating the Hippocampal STING-TBK1 Pathway.
post: Aim: Determine whether low-threshold intermittent hypoxia worsens LPS-induced depressive-like behaviour, cognitive deficits and hippocampal neuroinflammation. title: An examination of cerebellar perineuronal nets in major depression and child abuse
post: Aim: Test whether a history of child abuse alters perineuronal nets in the human dentate nucleus and in mouse deep cerebellar nuclei. post: Aim: To test whether auditory oddball responses and effective connectivity differ in adolescents at familial high risk for schizophrenia or bipolar disorder. title: Age-dependent structural brain aging in medication-free major depressive disorder: A multi-site analysis from COORDINATE-MDD consortium.
post: Aim: To test whether brain aging, measured as a brain age gap, is elevated in medication-free people with major depressive disorder and whether it depends on age and neuroanatomical phenotype. Methods: Harmonised T1-weighted MRI from 645 medication-free people with a current depressive episode and 645 matched healthy controls across 11 sites; gradient boosting brain age estimation with nested cross-validation and SHAP regional contributions. Results: Major depressive disorder was associated with a higher age-corrected brain age gap than controls (mean difference +2.0 years, Cohen's d -0.289). Gaps were absent before the mid-30s and reached +6.8 years in those aged 55 and older before site adjustment (4.3 years after). Conclusion: Structural brain aging in depression is age-dependent and strongest in a clinically vulnerable phenotype, consistent with but not establishing neuroprogression models.

title: Abnormalities and plasticity of white matter functional networks in opioid use disorder: a BOLD fMRI study.
post: Aim: To investigate architecture and activity of white matter functional networks in opioid use disorder and their change after prolonged abstinence. Methods: BOLD fMRI white matter signals analysed with k-means clustering in individuals with OUD at baseline and follow-up after prolonged abstinence, compared with healthy controls. Results: At baseline the deep frontoparietal network fragmented into the superior longitudinal fasciculus and anterior corona radiata networks, partially recovering after abstinence. Hyperactivation in the deep frontal network and hypoactivation in the frontotemporal-parietal network were present, with the latter negatively correlated with years of opioid use. Conclusion: OUD disrupts white matter network architecture and activity, while prolonged abstinence promotes partial restoration, indicating neuroplastic potential of white matter networks.

title: Gender- and season-specific neural signature revealed by resting EEG in major depressive disorder
post: Aim: Determine how gender and season jointly modulate resting EEG activity in major depressive disorder and whether EEG features predict symptom severity. Methods: Resting-state EEG from 132 people with MDD (67 women, 65 men, aged 18.66-78.00 years) across seasons; power spectral density, fuzzy entropy and transfer entropy; two-way ANOVA and Categorical Boosting regression with SHAP analysis. Results: Neural activity was modulated by gender and season, with peak divergence in winter or summer for women and spring for men. EEG features predicted Beck Depression Inventory scores with high accuracy (r = 0.9405 for women in winter). Conclusion: EEG features may serve as candidate biomarkers, and diagnosis may need to account for seasonal and gender-specific biological rhythms.

title: Proteomic profiling of postmortem prefrontal cortex identifies molecular signatures of borderline personality disorder
post: Aim: To characterise proteomic signatures of borderline personality disorder in postmortem prefrontal cortex. Methods: Label-free proteomics of postmortem prefrontal cortex in 79 individuals (36 with BPD, 43 controls); differential expression, co-expression network, druggability and drug-repositioning analyses; integration with PTSD and MDD datasets. A BPD-associated module enriched for secretory and synaptic processes was druggable by SSRIs, and STX7 and RTN4 were conserved differentially expressed proteins across BPD, PTSD and MDD. Conclusion: The study provides initial proteomic insights into BPD in the brain, suggests VEGF signalling as a possible target, and shows convergent signatures with common comorbidities.

title: The Role of TRPC6 in the Pathogenesis of Depression and Its Potential as a Therapeutic Target.
post: Aim: Clarify the role of TRPC6 calcium channels in depression and assess whether targeting them could yield antidepressant drugs. Methods: Narrative review of the latest research on TRPC6 function in depression, covering chronic stress models, hippocampal signalling and synaptic plasticity. title: Beyond Side Effects: The Role of Dissociation in Esketamine Therapy for Treatment-Resistant Depression.

post: Aim: To examine whether dissociation during intranasal esketamine therapy affects depressive outcomes in treatment-resistant depression. Methods: Retrospective chart review of 51 adults at an Israeli esketamine unit (2021-2025); DES-II trait dissociation, weekly PDEQ state dissociation, QIDS-SR16 severity; correlations and linear mixed-effects models. post: Aim: Whether adding ketamine to propofol as anaesthesia for electroconvulsive therapy improves depression and cognitive outcomes compared with propofol alone. Methods: Randomised controlled trial of 70 patients aged 18-65 with DSM-5 major depressive disorder receiving ECT, allocated to propofol 0.6 mg/kg plus ketamine 0.6 mg/kg or propofol 1.2 mg/kg; HAM-D and MMSE assessed before, after the first and after the third ECT course … Results: HAM-D scores were significantly lower after the third ECT in the ketamine-propofol group (F(1,58) = 23.24, p < 0.001), but no difference after the full ECT course. title: Intravenous ketamine for major depressive episodes in routine practice: a review of non-randomized evidence on effectiveness and safety.
post: Aim: To review non-randomised evidence on the effectiveness and safety of intravenous racemic ketamine for major depressive episodes in routine practice. Methods: Systematic searches of PubMed, Embase and PsycINFO to 30 September 2026; 56 non-randomised studies included. Results: Response ranged from 26% to 71% and remission from 14% to 53%, overlapping RCT estimates. Benefits often waned within weeks, attrition was high, blood pressure rises were transient, and serious adverse events and urinary and hepatic outcomes were poorly reported. Conclusion: Durability of benefit and cumulative safety of repeated IV ketamine remain uncertain; systematic safety monitoring and head-to-head and maintenance trials are needed.

post: Aim: To characterise longitudinal peripheral blood transcriptional changes during ECT and serial ketamine treatment in treatment-resistant depression. post: Aim: To describe ketamine-augmented hypnotherapy (KAHT) and report preliminary feasibility and outcome data from an uncontrolled case series. post: Aim: To test whether negative allosteric modulation of α5-GABAA receptors with basmisanil produces ketamine-like antidepressant actions via specific medial prefrontal cortex cell populations. title: Working memory neural correlates after ketamine in treatment-resistant depression: a randomized placebo-controlled functional magnetic resonance imaging study.

post: Aim: Test whether immediate TMS-evoked EEG potentials give a more direct measure of short-latency intracortical inhibition than MEP-based SICI. post: Aim: To characterise structural and functional reorganisation of the motor system in hemiplegic cerebral palsy and its links to lesion characteristics and upper-limb performance. post: Aim: Identify an early imaging biomarker of synaptic change after whole-brain radiation, to predict cognitive decline in a rodent model. title: SV2A PET imaging in Parkinson's disease and atypical parkinsonism: A systematic review of neuroimaging methodologies and regional findings.
post: Aim: To review neuroimaging methods and regional findings from SV2A PET in Parkinson's disease and atypical parkinsonian disorders. Methods: Systematic review following PRISMA 2020 of PubMed, Scopus and Web of Science; 14 studies using validated SV2A PET radiotracers in parkinsonian populations; risk of bias with QUADAS-2; narrative synthesis as heterogeneity precluded meta-analysis. Results: In PD the substantia nigra was most affected, with striatal involvement in advanced disease. In PSP and CBD synaptic loss was widespread and exceeded grey matter atrophy, falling about 3-4% per year in some longitudinal regions. In MSA infratentorial involvement predominated, with AUC up to 0.99. Conclusion: The authors conclude SV2A PET shows disease-specific presynaptic patterns supporting its use as a diagnostic and monitoring biomarker. They call for methodological harmonisation and longitudinal multicentre studies.

post: Aim: To determine how single-pulse TMS to the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex affects single-neuron activity in deep cortical and subcortical structures in humans. title: A staged microstructural mechanism of electroconvulsive therapy: disruption, potentiation, and rewiring.
post: Aim: Whether electroconvulsive therapy works through a staged process of disruption followed by neuroplastic potentiation and network rewiring, tested with longitudinal multishell diffusion MRI. Methods: Densely sampled longitudinal multishell diffusion MRI in 22 people with depression receiving ECT and 15 matched healthy controls, with scans before and after the first session, 7-14 days after the last session, and at 6 months; 141 scans analysed. Conclusion: The findings give in vivo human evidence for a staged disruption-rewiring process underlying ECT, a framework for how perturbation may become therapeutic reorganisation.

title: Sample size critically shapes the reliability of EEG case-control findings in psychiatry.
post: Aim: Quantify how sample size affects the reliability of EEG case-control findings across psychiatric conditions in children and adolescents. Methods: Resting-state EEG from 2,874 participants aged 5–18 years, including ADHD, autism, anxiety, learning disorders and controls, with spectral, temporal and complexity features compared across repeated random subsamples of varying size. Results: Small samples gave unstable, inflated and highly variable effect sizes, while larger samples converged on consistent but small effects. Statistical power rose steeply with sample size, while false positive rates stayed relatively stable. Conclusion: Sample size critically shapes EEG case-control outcomes, and conventional case-control designs may be limited for biomarker discovery in psychiatry.

Methods: Thesis combining a secondary qualitative analysis of 18 psychiatric outpatients with suicidal ideation treated with 12 sessions of web-based EMDR, and a mixed-methods single case study of 3MDR for PTSD in a person with dissociative identity disorder, with follow-up interviews. Results: Three existential themes emerged in the EMDR cohort: self-against-self, the anguish of being, and existential despair. In the 3MDR case, PTSD, anxiety and depression scores improved, with reported resolution of existential themes and post-traumatic growth. Conclusion: The authors suggest many people with chronic suicidality face existential crises rarely addressed in manualised therapies, and that adapted, transformative approaches may be needed. Findings come from a small sample and a single case.

title: Effects of 5-HT2A Receptor Activation on Oxycodone Demand after Short and Long Access Self-Administration in Male and Female Rats.
post: Aim: Whether 5-HT2A receptor activation by DOI reduces oxycodone demand after short or long access self-administration in male and female rats. Methods: Male and female Sprague-Dawley rats with jugular catheters self-administered oxycodone (0.1 mg/kg/infusion) under short or long access; DOI, volinanserin and SB242084 were tested using a threshold demand procedure with exponentiated demand analysis. Results: DOI dose-dependently reduced oxycodone demand in short-access rats in both sexes. After long access, low DOI doses reduced demand while the highest doses enhanced reinforcement; most effects were blocked by volinanserin, which itself reduced demand in long-access rats. Conclusion: Hallucinogenic 5-HT2A activation reduces oxycodone demand in a sex- and access-dependent way, and nonselective phenethylamines may prove less useful than selective agents.

title: Psilocybin-Assisted Therapy for Cancer-Related Psychological and Existential Distress in Adults with Cancer: An Integrative Systematic Review.
venue: Journal of pain & palliative care pharmacotherapy
venue_clean: Journal of pain & palliative care pharmacotherapy
post: Aim: Evaluates evidence on the safety, efficacy and therapeutic impact of psilocybin-assisted therapy for cancer-related psychological and existential distress. Methods: Integrative systematic review following PRISMA guidelines of 11 reports from six clinical cohorts, searched August to October 2025, with MMAT appraisal. Results: Single moderate-to-high psilocybin doses produced rapid, enduring reductions in depression, anxiety and existential distress lasting 2 to 6 months, and up to 4.5 years in some cases; no serious adverse events were reported. Conclusion: Psilocybin-assisted therapy may be promising for cancer-related distress but remains investigational, with several reports showing methodological limitations.

title: 5-HT2A receptor deletion is associated with reduced hippocampal parvalbumin levels and anxiety-like behavior in BALB/c mice
post: Aim: Investigates whether constitutive loss of 5-HT2A receptors alters anxiety-like behaviour and hippocampal parvalbumin interneuron proteins in BALB/c mice. Methods: Constitutive 5-HT2AR knockout in male and female BALB/c mice, behavioural anxiety paradigms, unbiased hippocampal proteomics, and perineuronal net component analysis; a separate cohort received the 5-HT2AR agonist 25CN-NBOH. Results: Knockout mice showed robust anxiety-like and repetitive behaviour, with reduced hippocampal parvalbumin and energy-metabolism proteins, and reduced HAPLN4, while aggrecan and HAPLN1 were unchanged. Conclusion: Loss of 5-HT2AR signalling is associated with coordinated reductions in parvalbumin and bioenergetic machinery without generalised loss of perineuronal net components.

title: The spatial distribution of glioblastoma correlates with specific neurotransmitter maps
post: Aim: To test whether the spatial distribution of glioblastoma follows the normative neurotransmitter and receptor architecture of the healthy brain. Methods: Retrospective study of 96 glioblastoma patients (mean age 62.2 years) from Padova University Hospital, with parcel-wise lesion frequency maps compared to normative PET neurotransmitter maps across two atlases using Neuromaps and spatially constrained null models. Results: Glioblastoma frequency correlated with dopaminergic, serotonergic and cholinergic systems, including 5-HT4 (ρ = 0.57, qFDR = 0.028), D2/D3 (ρ = 0.62, qFDR = 0.029) and DAT (r = 0.47, qFDR = 0.003). Higher expression of these neurotransmitters was associated with more frequent tumour occurrence. Conclusion: The authors conclude that the brain's neurochemical architecture may contribute to the spatial distribution of gliomas, consistent with gliomas integrating into functional neural networks. The design is correlational.
why_you: Directly relevant to your PET neurotransmitter mapping work, applying normative receptor maps to a clinical spatial question.

post: Aim: To develop and describe a trauma-informed readiness and risk assessment framework for community-based psychedelic-assisted therapy intake. title: Ketamine and psychedelics: A path to Alzheimer's disease prevention?
post: Aim: Whether ketamine and psychedelics can modulate mild cognitive impairment and Alzheimer's disease pathophysiology by regulating astrocyte mitochondria. Methods: Narrative review of literature on astrocyte metabolism, stress vulnerability and interactions with neurons, drawn from PubMed, Scopus and Google searches. Results: The reviewed literature suggests astrocyte-linked blood-brain barrier disruption, impaired glymphatic clearance, reduced glutamate uptake and synaptic loss can exacerbate amyloid-β accumulation and tau hyperphosphorylation. Ketamine and psychedelics may act on astrocyte mitochondria via NMDA, TrkB, sigma-1 and 5-HT2A receptors, potentially supporting neuronal metabolism. Conclusion: Astrocyte mitochondrial regulation offers a testable framework, but disease-modifying potential requires experimental validation and controlled clinical trials.

title: Cortical Hypoperfusion in Acute Anorexia Nervosa Is Graded Along the Sensorimotor-Association Hierarchy.
venue: The International journal of eating disorders
venue_clean: The International journal of eating disorders
post: Aim: To determine whether cortical hypoperfusion in acute anorexia nervosa is uniform or organised along the cortex's principal functional gradient, and whether it dissociates from cortical thinning. Methods: 44 acutely underweight women with anorexia nervosa and 45 healthy women underwent 3T pseudo-continuous arterial spin labelling with partial-volume correction, analysed across the Schaefer 100-region atlas and compared with cortical thickness and 18 PET/SPECT receptor maps. Results: Perfusion was lower in 97 of 100 regions, maximal in orbitofrontal and prefrontal cortex (composite d = -0.56). The deficit scaled with position along the principal functional gradient (ρ = -0.56), and hypoperfusion was greater where D1, CB1, mGluR5, M1, 5-HT2A and μ-opioid systems are dense. Conclusion: Cortical hypoperfusion in acute anorexia nervosa is graded along the sensorimotor-association axis, dissociable from thinning and aligned with reward-related neurochemistry. The cross-sectional design limits causal interpretation.
why_you: Combines cerebral blood flow, the principal functional gradient and receptor maps, closely matching your neurodynamics and PET neurochemistry interests.

title: Lysergic Acid Diethylamide Induces Transcriptional Changes Opposing Signatures of Brain Ageing and Neurodegeneration.
post: Aim: Asks whether LSD-induced transcriptional changes oppose gene expression signatures of brain ageing and dementia. Methods: Cross-species transcriptomic analysis of chronic LSD in rats and acute LSD in mice, compared with human prefrontal cortex ageing and dementia datasets, plus amyloid-beta experiments in primary cortical cultures. Results: LSD-induced profiles were strongly anti-correlated with human ageing signatures and, less strongly, with dementia signatures, and short-term LSD attenuated amyloid-beta-induced alterations. Conclusion: Provides a transcriptional rationale for investigating LSD and related compounds in brain ageing and neurodegeneration, pointing to mechanisms for future study.

title: A novel 5-HT2A receptor-linked signalling pathway involving NAADP-mediated lysosomal Ca2+ release
post: Aim: Establish whether the 5-HT2A receptor also signals through NAADP-mediated lysosomal calcium release. Methods: Measurement of cellular NAADP levels, pharmacological NAADP inhibition, direct lysosomal Ca2+ biosensor imaging with psychedelic agonists, and genetic ablation of the pathway in mouse models. NAADP pathway ablation reduced markers of hallucinogenic and neuroplastic effects in mice. Conclusion: A novel, therapeutically relevant signalling pathway is involved in psychedelic drug action, beyond the canonical G-protein and beta-arrestin routes.

title: Novel quantification method for psilocin in brain tissues using liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry.
venue: Analytical methods : advancing methods and applications
venue_clean: Analytical methods : advancing methods and applications
post: Aim: Develops and validates an LC-MS/MS method to quantify psilocin and 4-HIAA in brain tissue. Methods: Chromatography-centred LC-MS/MS approach with matrix dilution, shallower gradient and diverter-valve timing, applied to mouse brain sections from psilocybin and psilocin co-crystal dosing. title: Role of Pineal Gland and Melatonin Dysregulation in Autism Spectrum Disorder with a Critical Appraisal of the Endogenous N, N-dimethyltryptamine Hypothesis: A Systematic Review
venue: Journal of Anatomical Society of India
venue_clean: Journal of Anatomical Society of India
post: Aim: Review pineal and melatonin dysregulation in autism spectrum disorder and critically appraise the endogenous DMT hypothesis. Methods: PRISMA 2020 systematic review of PubMed, Scopus, Embase and Web of Science records (2000 to May 2025), with 22 primary studies included and evidence graded with GRADE. Results: Melatonin dysregulation is supported by observational, genetic and clinical evidence, while pineal morphology rests on one neuroimaging study. No included study examined endogenous DMT directly in ASD; the two relevant reports were preclinical. Conclusion: Melatonin-pathway dysfunction is an evidence-supported contributor to ASD-related sleep disturbance, whereas the DMT hypothesis remains theoretical and needs direct human study.

title: Autistic adults’ attitudes toward ketamine, MDMA, LSD, psilocybin and antidepressants: a cross-sectional survey
post: Aim: Describe how Autistic adults perceive harm, efficacy and willingness to try psilocybin, MDMA, ketamine, LSD and antidepressants. Methods: Cross-sectional anonymous online survey of 128 Autistic adults (October 2021 to July 2022), rating each substance, with paired comparisons and exploratory associations with self-medication. Results: Psilocybin had the highest proportions endorsing no harm, high efficacy and willingness to try, and differed from the other substances on several measures. Willingness was 17.2 to 21.1 points higher under doctor than peer recommendation. Conclusion: Autistic adults reported more favourable attitudes to psilocybin than antidepressants; these are perceptions, not evidence of comparative efficacy, and recommendation source may matter.

title: DMT-induced aberrant salience and suggestibility correlate with mystical experiences and positive emotionality
post: Aim: To test whether DMT-induced aberrant salience and suggestibility relate to mystical and emotional psychedelic experiences. Methods: Randomised, placebo-controlled, double-blind crossover study in 25 healthy participants receiving inhaled DMT (60 mg) or active placebo (0.6 mg), with aberrant salience, suggestibility and psychedelic experience questionnaires. Results: Compared with placebo, DMT increased all aberrant salience factors, most suggestibility modalities and most psychedelic factors. Aberrant salience correlated widely with psychedelic experiences, particularly mystical and positive emotional factors. Conclusion: DMT induces both psychosis- and therapy-relevant processes, with the link to mystical experience possibly indirect and emotionality playing a more central role.

title: Psilocybin Reconfigures Cortical Dynamics Across Temporal, Spatial, and Hierarchical Scales
post: Aim: Clarify the spatial and temporal origins of increased signal irregularity in psychedelic fMRI studies. Methods: Brain entropy was quantified with sample entropy in 57 paired PsiConnect participants and tested against BOLD surrogates (zero-lag covariance and phase randomisation), with replication in a seven-person crossover cohort. Results: Spatial and temporal entropy rose after psilocybin with reduced local synchrony and shorter intrinsic timescales. Surrogates reproduced the spatial and temporal entropy changes, and the measured increases recurred in the replication cohort. Conclusion: Linking entropy to spatial coordination and temporal persistence explains how psilocybin reorganises cortical dynamics across scales.

title: Unmixing the psychedelic connectome: Brain network traits of psilocybin.
post: Aim: Test whether the psilocybin-induced connectome is a composite of dissociable connectivity patterns rather than one global change. Methods: Connectome independent component analysis with multilevel resampling applied to resting-state fMRI from healthy volunteers given psilocybin, relating traits to plasma psilocin and a divergent thinking task. Conclusion: The acute psilocybin state appears to involve co-occurring, dissociable connectivity patterns, supporting decompositional connectomic approaches.

title: Ayahuasca and Major Depressive Disorder: Examining the Role of the Default Mode Network in Its Therapeutic Potential
post: Aim: Examine the role of the default mode network in the therapeutic potential of ayahuasca for major depressive disorder. Methods: Narrative review of PubMed and Google Scholar literature on DMN connectivity in depression and on the neurological and clinical effects of ayahuasca and DMT, prioritising primary research. title: A Translational Porcine Model Linking Brain 5-HT2A Receptor Occupancy to Psychedelic-like Behaviour
post: Aim: Establish a translational pig model that links drug dose and plasma concentration to brain 5-HT2A receptor occupancy, so that behavioural doses can be chosen pharmacologically. Methods: Pigs were dosed with five 5-HT2A agonists and two antagonists; brain 5-HT2A occupancy was measured with [11C]Cimbi-36 PET and in vitro, and headshake behaviour was recorded at occupancy levels tied to psychedelic experience in humans. Results: Occupancy correspondence with human data was good across compounds. At human-relevant occupancy, all five agonists induced headshakes, including lisuride and 2-Br-LSD, which are otherwise considered non-psychedelic. Conclusion: Human-relevant 5-HT2A occupancy produces psychedelic-like behaviour in pigs, validating the model for translational dosing of novel 5-HT2A compounds.

title: Cortical dynamics during psychedelic and anesthetized states induced by ketamine
post: Aim: To characterise how the spatiotemporal complexity of EEG activity changes across subanesthetic and anaesthetic doses of ketamine. Methods: High-density scalp EEG in healthy volunteers during subanesthetic and anaesthetic ketamine. Hidden Markov modelling classified brain states, and Lempel-Ziv complexity was computed per state after controlling for spectral changes. Results: Subanesthetic ketamine raised complexity relative to baseline. Anaesthetic ketamine produced alternating low and high complexity before stabilising at a high level comparable to baseline. Conclusion: Ketamine-induced state transitions share features of anaesthesia, normal consciousness and altered consciousness, illustrating its complex pharmacological properties.

title: A Single Dose of Psilocybin Increases Synaptic Density and Decreases 5-HT2A Receptor Density in the Pig Brain
post: Aim: To test whether a single psilocybin dose changes synaptic density (SV2A) and 5-HT2A receptor density in the pig brain. Methods: Twenty-four awake pigs received psilocybin 0.08 mg/kg or saline intravenously and were euthanised at one or seven days. Autoradiography of hippocampus and prefrontal cortex used [3H]UCB-J, [3H]MDL100907 and [3H]Cimbi-36. Results: One day after psilocybin, hippocampal SV2A density was 4.42% higher and 5-HT2A density was lower in hippocampus and prefrontal cortex (−15.21% to −50.19%), significant for hippocampus across ligands and for prefrontal cortex with Cimbi-36 only. At seven days SV2A remained higher (+9.24% hippocampus, +6.10% prefrontal cortex), with no 5-HT2A differences. Conclusion: Psilocybin may cause persistent synaptogenesis and an acute fall in 5-HT2A density, possibly contributing to antidepressant effects.
why_you: Directly relevant to your synaptic density PET ([11C]UCB-J) and 5-HT2A work, providing a preclinical benchmark for psilocybin plasticity.

title: A neural code for generative speech production in human Wernicke's area.
post: Aim: Does Wernicke's area, classically linked to speech comprehension, also contribute to generating speech, and if so, what does it encode? Methods: Direct intracranial recordings in human patients, cortical stimulation and lesion analysis, examining activity before speech and causal necessity for production. Results: A discrete subzone, the left posterior superior temporal gyrus, activates before speech, is causally necessary for production, and encodes features of whole upcoming words rather than low-level acoustics or articulation. Its activity differs from nearby auditory-feedback responses and can decode intended speech in people with paralysis. Conclusion: Wernicke's area contains a dedicated subregion for speech generation alongside its role in auditory processing.
why_you: Adds a causal human-cortex perspective on how a region's perceptual role coexists with production, relevant to your interest in neurodynamics and whole-brain organisation.

title: A glucose-powered artificial neuroimmune axis for metabolic control.
post: Aim: Whether a battery-free, glucose-powered artificial neuroimmune axis can restore metabolic and immune balance through closed-loop vagal-like stimulation. Methods: NeuroAxis, a closed-loop device powered by endogenous glucose with metabolic interoceptive feedback, tested in rat models of type 1 and type 2 diabetes. Conclusion: The authors propose NeuroAxis as a general approach for autonomous interorgan regulation, based on rodent models.

title: The fate of poised pre-mRNAs shapes mitochondrial activity and cellular differentiation.
post: Aim: To determine how nuclear RNA quality control decides the fate of poised intron-containing polyadenylated pre-mRNAs. Methods: Molecular and genetic study in mouse and human cells, including NCBP3 depletion and pathogenic RNA exosome mutations, with analysis of mitochondrial function and motor behaviour. Results: NCBP3 favours splicing of poised pre-mRNAs while anillin favours exosome degradation; many affected transcripts encode mitochondrial factors. NCBP3 loss or exosome mutations reduced mitochondrial activity, causing muscle weakness, cerebellar hypomyelination and poorer motor coordination. Conclusion: A competition between pre-mRNA pathways controls mitochondrial function, and its disruption contributes to neurological disease.
why_you: Only loosely relevant to your fields; a neuroscientist might find the link between mitochondrial gene regulation and cerebellar disease of interest.

title: Injury-induced signalling coordinates immunity and cannibalism in locusts.
post: Aim: To identify the molecular signal that draws cannibalistic locusts to injured conspecifics. Methods: Behavioural assays, olfactory receptor knockdowns, and bacterial gene-cluster deletions in Locusta migratoria, examining the symbiont-derived volatile guaiacol. Results: Guaiacol, released more after injury, attracts nymphs and triggers cannibalism via receptors LmOR36 and LmOR34. It is made by the symbiont Enterobacter hormaechei; deleting its gene cluster abolished production and behavioural effects. At low levels it activates immune pathways. Conclusion: A microbial-chemical signal links immune defence with cannibalism, offering molecular targets for population manipulation.

post: Aim: Determine how psilocybin and ketamine reshape perceptual decision-making and orbitofrontal population dynamics in mice. title: Animal models in psychedelic research - Tripping over translation.
post: Aim: To audit how rodent psychedelic studies are designed and whether their conditions and assays could translate to human therapy. Methods: Systematic review of 266 rodent psychedelic studies published 2014 to 2026, assessing welfare and set-and-setting-like factors, behavioural assay design, and individual and social factors. Results: Most studies included stress-inducing factors: only 14% tested in the active phase, 7% used environmental enrichment, and 21% used refined handling. Drug administration almost universally used restraint-requiring methods. Most assays were brief and isolated, and group-level cross-sectional designs dominated. Conclusion: The authors argue translation requires longitudinal tracking of individuals in enriched social settings with comprehensive behavioural characterisation.
why_you: Directly relevant to your psychedelic clinical pharmacology and preclinical translation questions, including how set and setting shape human outcomes.

Global criticality, with scale-free avalanches and optimal functional connectivity, emerged only when local populations were near criticality and coupled within an optimal range. Conclusion: Local and global criticality are dynamically intertwined but not directly aligned, and their relationship depends on structural connectivity.

title: Spectral and complexity-based signatures of advanced concentration absorption meditation: A high-density EEG study of jhana
post: Aim: To characterise spectral and entropy-based EEG signatures of each jhana state of advanced concentration absorption meditation and relate them to experience. title: Bridging Treatment Gaps in Adolescent Depression With Neuromodulation Targeting Anhedonia
post: Aim: Whether individualised functional connectivity-guided iTBS targeting left DLPFC improves depression and anhedonia in adolescents who have not responded to antidepressants. Methods: Commentary on a randomised, double-blind, sham-controlled trial of individualised iTBS in adolescents with major depressive disorder, with the target chosen by connectivity to the nucleus accumbens. title: The Potency Stability Tradeoff: Evaluating EEG Biomarkers for Major Depressive Disorder.
post: Aim: Whether EEG biomarkers for major depressive disorder that are stable across data subsets generalise better than those with the strongest predictive signal. Methods: EEG from 30 MDD patients and 88 controls; connectivity, spectral and complexity features; XGBoost pipeline with leakage-free cross-validation and a nested Stability-Optimized Consensus Learning framework. Results: Theta and alpha features gave the strongest signal (max AUC 0.683) but were unstable across subsets (mean Jaccard 0.187) and overfitted. A model built on stable consensus biomarkers generalised better (AUC 0.792 vs 0.662) with less overfitting (P < .05). Conclusion: The MDD signature exists as a potent but unstable theta-alpha signal and a weaker but stable connectome signal. The authors argue stability matters more than strength for clinical biomarkers.
why_you: Speaks to the reliability of EEG markers in depression, a question central to your EEG and computational psychiatry work.

title: Bergenin ameliorates anxiety- and depression-like behavior in antibiotic-treated mice: behavioral and in silico insights.
post: Aim: Whether bergenin, an anti-inflammatory isocoumarin, reverses anxiety- and depression-like behaviour induced by antibiotic-driven gut dysbiosis in mice. Methods: Antibiotic regimen in Swiss albino mice followed by 14 days of bergenin (25 or 50 mg/kg/day) or fluoxetine; elevated plus maze, open field, forced swim and tail suspension tests; docking and 100 ns molecular dynamics against TLR4-MD-2 and SERT. Results: Bergenin dose-dependently attenuated anxiety- and depression-like deficits, with high-dose recovery of about 70-92%, without altering behaviour in antibiotic-free animals. In silico, it bound the SERT S1 site with stability resembling fluoxetine, but its TLR4-MD-2 interaction was shallow. Conclusion: Bergenin ameliorates behavioural deficits in antibiotic-treated mice, and in silico data favour serotonergic over TLR4 involvement. The authors stress that the work is hypothesis-generating and that microbiome and mechanistic assays were not performed.
why_you: Gut-brain and serotonergic mechanisms in mood fit your interest in brain-body coupling, though the link is indirect.

title: Connectome Harmonic Analysis at 7 Tesla Reveals Selective Reorganization of Large-Scale Cortical Dynamics in Adult Users of Cannabis.
post: Aim: Whether cannabis use alters large-scale brain organisation, tested as changes in low-frequency connectome harmonics using 7T resting-state fMRI. Methods: Human Connectome Project 7T data from 81 cannabis users and 81 matched non-users; BOLD activity projected onto the first 200 connectome harmonics; t-tests with FDR correction and atlas localisation. Results: Cannabis users showed significantly greater power in one low-frequency harmonic (k = 6; t ≈ 4.19; p_FDR = 7.21 × 10⁻³; d = 0.659), roughly 44% higher than non-users, localised to a frontoparietal–sensorimotor network. It did not correlate with cannabis exposure variables, and behavioural associations did not survive FDR correction. Conclusion: Cannabis use is associated with selective amplification of one frontoparietal–sensorimotor eigenmode. The authors note the behavioural findings are nominal only.

post: Aim: How demographics and polysubstance use patterns differ between people with primary cocaine and methamphetamine use disorders screened for a TMS trial. Methods: Screening data from 320 participants in NIDA CTN-0108 (120 with cocaine use disorder, 200 with methamphetamine use disorder), comparing demographics and substance use patterns. title: Mechanism-aligned ketamine therapy for treatment-resistant depression: a 2026 update—toward an integrative mechanistic framework for clinical translation
post: Aim: Propose an integrative mechanistic framework for ketamine therapy in treatment-resistant depression, updating a 2021 systems-level model with literature through April 2026. Methods: Narrative review integrating evidence on NMDAR modulation, neuroplastogenesis, anti-inflammatory signalling, entropic brain states and psychedelic phenomenology, with attention to chronic stress and attachment as cross-cutting factors. post: Aim: Whether source-level EEG measures distinguish active from sham single-pulse TMS over the left DLPFC at early and late latencies. Methods: Thirty-three healthy adults underwent active and sham TMS-EEG; analyses included TEPs, electric-field simulations, source-level SCD and SCS in target ROIs, whole-brain cluster permutation tests, and peripheral covariate adjustment after ICA. title: Selective distal upper extremity recovery following targeted dentate nucleus temporal interference stimulation in stroke-double-blind, sham-controlled randomized controlled trial with resting-state EEG
post: Aim: Whether dentate nucleus-targeted temporal interference stimulation improves upper limb recovery after subacute stroke, with resting-state EEG as the main neurophysiological outcome. title: OPM-MEG is characterized by increased sensitivity for visual gamma-band oscillations: A parallel EEG/OPM-MEG study
post: Aim: Whether OPM-MEG detects visually induced gamma-band oscillations with higher sensitivity than EEG. Methods: Simultaneous EEG and OPM-MEG recordings in 26 participants during a visual grating task; gamma (30–80 Hz) and alpha/beta power and inter-trial phase coherence compared across modalities, with effect sizes as Cohen's dz. Alpha/beta changes and ITPC showed no consistent modality difference. Conclusion: OPM-MEG offers enhanced sensitivity for visual gamma oscillations relative to EEG, which may support more precise study of cortical circuit function.

title: Feasibility of Simulated Low-Count [18F]FDG PET/MR for Patients with Pediatric Epilepsy.
post: Aim: To test whether simulated low-count [18F]FDG PET/MR preserves diagnostic quality and epileptogenic zone lateralisation in paediatric epilepsy. Methods: Twenty-seven paediatric patients with epilepsy; list-mode data truncated to simulate 50%, 65% and 80% count reductions, analysed with ROI- and voxel-based lateralisation methods. Results: Contrast-to-noise fell and coefficient of variation rose with count reduction. Image quality stayed clinically acceptable up to 65% reduction, with consistent SUVRs and unchanged lateralisation agreement with the clinical consensus. Conclusion: A 65% simulated count reduction preserved acceptable image quality and lateralisation in paediatric epilepsy, supporting future lower-activity validation studies.

title: Tracking single neurons across days reveals acute and persistent effects of psilocybin in the mouse brain
post: Aim: Whether psilocybin's effects on single-neuron firing extend beyond the acute drug presence, and how acute responses relate to lasting changes. Methods: Chronically implanted Neuropixels probes in mice tracked 1,692 neurons in prefrontal and hippocampal regions after saline and psilocybin injections and again 24 h later. Results: Psilocybin bidirectionally modulated firing acutely in a cell-type and region-specific manner. Firing 24 h post-injection was net suppressed relative to saline, including in acutely activated neurons, and the late acute response predicted later firing. Conclusion: The authors present the first direct evidence of psilocybin's sustained effects on neuronal firing, offering insight into circuitry behind its lasting alterations.

title: Psychedelic experience intensity during ketamine treatment and antidepressant outcomes.
post: Aim: Test whether subjective psychedelic intensity during ketamine treatment is associated with antidepressant outcomes beyond an adverse-event framing. Methods: Retrospective longitudinal cohort of 3,637 adults with moderate-to-severe depression receiving up to four sublingual ketamine doses over four weeks, with subjective effects measured by the five-item Mindbloom Psychedelic Intensity scale at midpoint. Results: Higher intensity scores at two weeks were associated with greater PHQ-9 reduction at four weeks, higher likelihood of clinically significant change, and greater membership of an improvement trajectory, independent of dose and covariates. Conclusion: Subjective intensity of the ketamine experience is robustly associated with antidepressant response, although the retrospective design limits causal inference.

title: Reconsidering the Psychotomimetic Properties of LSD: Connectome-Based Classification Reveals Partial Overlap with First Episode Psychosis
post: Aim: Compare the acute effects of LSD with medication-naive first episode psychosis on resting-state functional connectivity using connectome-based classification. title: Psychedelics and Sleep: Preclinical and Human Studies-A Systematic Review.
post: Aim: To review preclinical and human evidence on how classic psychedelics (LSD, psilocybin, DMT/ayahuasca) alter sleep architecture, sleep quality, EEG activity and dreams. Methods: PRISMA-guided systematic review of PubMed up to May 2026; twelve eligible preclinical and clinical studies, with validity assessed by appropriate quality tools. Results: Preclinical studies consistently showed acute REM suppression, delayed REM onset and increased wakefulness. Human findings were heterogeneous: psilocybin prolonged REM latency, ayahuasca reduced REM duration, and slow-wave activity results were mixed. Conclusion: Classic psychedelics cause acute but transient sleep changes, mainly in REM sleep. Whether these contribute to therapeutic effects is uncertain, and the review was not prospectively registered.
why_you: Your work on psychedelic clinical pharmacology and EEG markers makes the REM and slow-wave findings directly relevant to psilocybin and DMT studies.

title: Psilocybin induces delayed and dynamic changes in human sleep neurophysiology: Results from a randomized controlled trial of psilocybin assisted therapy in patients with comorbid major depressive and alcohol use disorder
post: Aim: Characterise the acute and post-acute temporal dynamics of sleep neurophysiology after psilocybin-assisted therapy in comorbid depression and alcohol use disorder. Methods: Randomised placebo-controlled trial with 40 participants (psilocybin n=22, placebo n=18), home sleep EEG for three nights before and seven nights after administration, analysed with nonlinear mixed-effects models. Results: Delayed, nonlinear changes emerged after psilocybin, with NREM slow-wave activity, sigma and REM beta peaking or troughing around 3–4 nights post-administration. Sleep efficiency and total sleep time increased over the first three post-treatment nights, while architecture changes were largely absent. Conclusion: Psilocybin-assisted therapy induces delayed, dynamic sleep EEG changes beyond the acute period, suggesting sleep EEG may be a sensitive measure of evolving neurophysiology.

post: Aim: Determine how psilocybin and escitalopram reshape brain dynamics in depression, and whether vortex-space modelling captures treatment effects better than signal-space modelling. Psilocybin increased vortex-space effective connectivity and reduced modularity, whereas escitalopram showed no comparable change. Greater increases in brain turbulence were associated with symptom reduction in both treatments. Conclusion: The two treatments reorganise brain dynamics in markedly different ways yet share features linked to clinical improvement, and vortex-space modelling is a promising framework for depression.

title: Psilocybin desynchronizes the human brain
post: Aim: To determine how psilocybin reshapes large-scale human brain functional connectivity and whether these changes relate to the subjective experience and lasting effects. Methods: Longitudinal precision fMRI with roughly 18 scans per participant in healthy adults, before, during and for three weeks after 25 mg psilocybin or 40 mg methylphenidate, with a further psilocybin dose 6-12 months later. Results: Psilocybin produced over threefold greater acute connectivity change than methylphenidate, driven by cross-scale desynchronisation, strongest in the default mode network. Anterior hippocampus to default mode connectivity stayed reduced for weeks. Conclusion: Persistent hippocampal-default mode reduction may be a neuroanatomical correlate of the proplasticity and therapeutic effects of psychedelics. The sample is small and healthy-volunteer based.

title: Human land use drives microplastic abundance in terrestrial wildlife.
authors: Marcia de Almeida Monteiro Melo Ferraz
post: Aim: To determine how human land use and the animals' proximity to development shape microplastic burdens in terrestrial wildlife. Methods: In vivo microplastic measurements in blood and tissue of free-ranging lowland tapirs and giant anteaters across Brazil, paired with high-resolution GPS tracking and human footprint exposure data. title: Domain-level symptom improvement after ketamine and TMS-based stimulation in treatment-resistant depression: a post hoc pooled analysis.
post: Aim: Whether ketamine and TMS produce different short-term improvements across depression, anxiety, insomnia and somatic symptom domains. title: FDTest: Fluctuation-dissipation theorem as a test for memory effects in brain dynamics.
post: Aim: Whether a generalised fluctuation-dissipation theorem can detect local memory effects in whole-brain dynamics and distinguish wakefulness from deep sleep. title: Exploring subacute effects of a DMT and harmine meditation retreat on the brain's control energy landscape
post: Aim: Whether a DMT and harmine meditation retreat changes the brain's control energy landscape in the subacute afterglow window. Methods: Exploratory analysis of rs-fMRI from a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (N = 39) before and after a three-day retreat, with control energy computed on a group structural connectome under two timescale approaches. Methods: 64-channel EEG in 25 experienced breathwork practitioners, with resting-state recordings interleaved through a naturalistic high-ventilation breathwork session; experience depth and content also recorded. Conclusion: The authors argue these are shared neural features of psychedelic-like states regardless of induction method, so breathwork may access psychedelic-like cortical states without drugs.

Conclusion: This article aims to provide the field with a comprehensive overview that can propel future research in such a way as to elucidate the neurocognitive mechanisms of psychedelics.

title: Chronic Mild Stress in Male Wistar-Kyoto Rats Induces Long-Term Hippocampal Plasticity Impairments Differentially Reversed by Acute and Chronic Ketamine Treatment.
post: Aim: Here, we investigated how chronic mild stress and subsequent acute and chronic ketamine treatments modulate synaptic plasticity in the Schaffer collateral pathway in the dorsal hippocampus of stress-vulnerable Wistar-Kyoto rats. post: Background: Ketamine produces rapid antidepressant effects in treatment-resistant depression (TRD), but these benefits diminish within days. title: Repeated prefrontal transcranial direct current stimulation improves behavioral regulation and modulates resting-state EEG microstate dynamics in young adults with problematic smartphone use: a randomized sham-controlled longitudinal study.

title: Gender differences in depressive-like behavior in Parkinson's disease.
post: Background: Although sex differences have been described in PD progression, the mechanisms underlying gender-specific susceptibility to depressive symptoms remain poorly understood. title: Endogenous suspension of phenomenal consciousness during extended cessation: Regional homogeneity analysis of multi-participant 7T fMRI of an advanced meditative endpoint.
post: Background: Extended cessation (EC) is a rare advanced meditative state characterized by the voluntary absence of reportable phenomenal experience, followed by reproducible aftereffects including immense mental clarity, equanimity, and peace. Methods: In a small-N case study (N = 3) using ultra-high-resolution 7T functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) with dense within-subject sampling, we quantified whole-brain activity and related it to chemoarchitecture and cognitive maps. Results: EC is marked by increased activity in unimodal sensory cortices and viscerosensory brainstem nuclei, and down-regulation in transmodal regions, subcortex and brainstem. Multivariate coupling to normative neurotransmitter maps revealed that EC-related connectivity changes covaried with histaminergic H 3 receptors topology. Conclusion: These findings constrain prevailing theories of consciousness by demonstrating that loss of experience need not entail global neural suppression, and supports accounts emphasizing selective precision modulation and hierarchical decoupling.

title: Mechanism-guided generative chemistry yields distinct agonist-like and antagonist-like ligand populations for the serotonin 5-HT2A receptor
post: Background: Designing serotonin 5-HT2A receptor ligands with a specified functional direction is difficult because binding affinity, assay-derived mechanism labels, molecular properties and receptor conformation are only partially coupled.
